extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, newsroom leaders, journalism educators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for journalists and newsrooms on adopting constructive journalism: an editorial approach that foregrounds solutions, nuance, and democratic conversation across reporting workflows and formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight responses to well-documented problems by reporting on efforts to solve them; change the story focus from the problem itself to potential and real responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be rigorous and critical when covering solutions — verify claims, assess effectiveness, and provide context. The aim is not activism or feel‑good reporting; avoid promoting a single solution. Related approach: solutions journalism (emphasizes this pillar). Example tools/case: NDR radio guidance on incorporating solution-focused stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover nuances (embrace complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Return reporting to balanced, fair, and non-sensational approaches that present issues in a complexity-aware, contextualized way rather than black-and-white terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a calm tone, reduce tabloid-style scandalizing and outrage, and prioritize complete, nuanced narratives that help the public develop an accurate understanding. Example: Berlingske (Denmark) guidance on nuance in political coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote democratic conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Strengthen democracy by promoting civil discourse, engaging audiences, and building trust without taking sides or inflaming polarization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitate critical but constructive debate about potential solutions; enable and report on dialogic initiatives that bridge divides (e.g., ZEIT ONLINE’s My Country Talks pairing). Avoid amplifying partisan agendas; prioritize formats that foster deliberation and mutual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story selection: include 'What Now?'
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing stories, go beyond the classic 5 W's (Who, What, When, Where, Why) to add 'What Now?' — i.e., what are possible next steps, responses, or solutions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize topics where reporting can illuminate responses, implementation challenges, or avenues for public action. This reframes coverage to be forward-looking and useful for audiences making real decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviews: shift from accusatory to curious and open-minded
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct interviews in a curious, exploratory manner rather than purely accusatory or adversarial questioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask questions that surface context, trade‑offs, and possible solutions; use open-minded probing to understand actors’ incentives and constraints. This supports nuance and reduces performative confrontation while maintaining accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and tone: curious, calm, and non-sensational
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a writing and presentation style that is calm, curious, and avoids sensationalist dramatization or outrage-driven language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move away from dramatic hooks that prioritize emotion over accuracy. Tone should foster understanding and engagement without trivializing or sugar-coating serious issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalist role: facilitator (beyond policeman and judge)
rubrics_metrics.description: After documenting evidence (policeman) and investigating/judging (judge), the constructive journalist also takes on a facilitator role seeking ways beyond the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitate conversations with experts, those in power, and affected communities about responses and solutions; act as a conduit for constructive public dialogue while still preserving critical scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply constructive lens across beats (including politics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use constructive practices in political coverage by focusing less on horse‑race metrics (polls/fundraising) and more on the concrete information voters need to decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift political stories toward policy substance, implementation details, and the real-world impacts of proposals — steering discussion away from partisan talking points toward concrete proposals addressing societal challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate with breaking and investigative journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism should act as an additional layer that complements breaking and investigative reporting rather than replacing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First fulfill watchdog roles (expose and investigate problems); then add reporting that explores responses, reform pathways, and lessons learned so audiences get the full picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be rigorous and critical about both problems and progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain the same journalistic standards of evidence, skepticism, and verification when reporting on proposed or promising solutions as when exposing problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess efficacy, unintended consequences, scalability, and evidence behind solutions. Avoid uncritical optimism; subject solutions to the same scrutiny as claims of wrongdoing or failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address important societal issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize reporting on issues that matter to society and democratic life rather than trivial or purely sensational topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select stories with clear public interest, policy relevance, or substantial community impact; ensure coverage helps citizens make informed decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be factual and unbiased
rubrics_metrics.description: Base reporting on verified facts and strive for impartiality and fairness in presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use credible sources, provide context, disclose uncertainties, and avoid partisan framing. Fact-based reporting underpins trust and democratic function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridge rather than polarize
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for reporting that connects different viewpoints and reduces polarization rather than inflaming divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight common ground, explain trade-offs, and report on dialogues and initiatives that bring opposing views together (e.g., facilitated conversations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward-looking and future-oriented coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Orient stories toward the future implications, potential outcomes, and next steps rather than solely chronicling past mistakes or present conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include analyses of trajectories, policy options, and what successful or failed responses might mean moving forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nuanced and contextualized reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide context, history, data, and multiple perspectives so audiences understand complexity and avoid simplistic conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use background reporting, expert analysis, and relevant data to situate current events within broader trends and explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist sensationalism and outrage-driven algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid coverage that intentionally provokes outrage or leverages clickbait tactics that distort public perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design headlines, leads, and social distribution to reflect accuracy and nuance rather than maximize short-term engagement via sensational framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid promoting a specific agenda or engaging in activism
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not blur the line between journalism and political advocacy; constructive journalism is not activism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report on solutions and debates without advocating for particular actors or policies. Present competing options and evidence so audiences can draw informed conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uncritical or naive reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t present solutions or actors in an unexamined, overly positive light without assessing evidence and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include caveats, discuss uncertainties, and investigate possible downsides or failures of proposed responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid glorifying individuals, governments, or organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from hero-worship or promotional coverage of specific people or institutions as sole sources of solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on actions, evidence, and systems rather than personality-driven narratives; interrogate claims and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not suppress critical perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive reporting should still surface critical viewpoints and hold power to account rather than glossing over problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance solution-focused coverage with investigative questions and accountability reporting; present dissenting evidence when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not give in to false equivalence or oversimplified balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid creating false balance by giving equal weight to unsupported or fringe positions in the name of neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh claims according to evidence; contextualize minority views instead of elevating them to parity with well-supported positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid advocating one solution over others or oversimplifying complex problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present a single remedy as the obvious or exclusive answer, nor reduce complex issues to simplistic fixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report on multiple approaches, trade-offs, and implementation challenges; interrogate what evidence supports each option and where uncertainties remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dialogue- and solutions-oriented methods where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate related approaches such as dialogue journalism and solutions journalism to engage audiences and examine responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ formats that foster audience participation, civil debate, and evidence-based examination of interventions (e.g., moderated dialogues, solution case studies). Examples: ZEIT ONLINE’s My Country Talks; NRK’s civil political debate show.
